1199	
1200	## 15. Resume Semantics
1201	
1202	`crates/deadreckon/src/main.rs:18484` is the `resume_command` handler.
1203	
1204	### 15.1 The Completed guard
1205	
1206	`main.rs:18493`:
1207	
1208	```rust
1209	if state.status == RunStatus::Completed {
1210	    println!("run {} is already completed", state.run_id);
1211	    return Ok(());
1212	}
1213	```
1214	
1215	Completed runs cannot be resumed. They can be re-promoted (idempotent) but not re-entered into the loop. The only forward path for a completed run today is to start a new run.
1216	
1217	### 15.2 The replay process
1218	
1219	For non-Completed runs (`Failed`, `Killed`, `Paused`):
1220	
1221	1. Acquire the task lock.
1222	2. Clear `failure_reason`, `pause_reason`, `killed_at`.
1223	3. Set `status = Planned`.
1224	4. Optionally extend `max_wall_seconds` from the resume flag.
1225	5. Set `child_pids = vec![cli_pid]`.
1226	6. `save_state()`.
1227	7. Call `run_turn_loop` with `RunLoopConfig.from_turn = <CLI flag>`.
1228	8. The loop calls `load_or_reconstruct_history(state, from_turn)` in `crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs`, which loads `history.json` if present, else reconstructs from `traces.jsonl`. With `from_turn = N`, history is truncated to N entries and `state.turn = N`.
1229	
1230	History reconstruction tolerates a `traces.jsonl` that ends mid-tool-call by ignoring incomplete entries — the next turn re-runs that turn.
1231	
1232	See `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/RESUME-SEMANTICS.md` for the contract.
1233

1235	
1236	## 16. Cross-Tool Import
1237	
1238	`deadreckon import <source>` reads from external coding-agent histories and synthesizes a completed deadreckon run from one concrete imported session, or from an explicit `--all` root import. It is read-only with respect to provider-owned transcript roots and writes only deadreckon run-state files.
1239	
1240	Today's sources:
1241	
1242	| Source | Discovery | Format |
1243	|---|---|---|
1244	| `codex` / `cli:codex` | `cli:codex` descriptor `[ingest]`, including `CODEX_SESSIONS_DIR`, `session_meta.payload.cwd`, `*.jsonl`, and `codex-cli` schema | JSONL |
1245	| `claude-code` / `cli:claude-code` | `cli:claude-code` descriptor `[ingest]`, including `CLAUDE_PROJECTS_DIR` and Claude project-directory cwd mapping | JSONL |
1246	| `gemini` / `cli:gemini` | `cli:gemini` descriptor `[ingest]`, including `GEMINI_DIR`, JSON/JSONL storage, and `gemini` schema | JSON or JSONL |
1247	| `opencode` / `cli:opencode` | `cli:opencode` descriptor `[ingest]`, file-mode `storage/session`, `storage/message`, and `storage/part` | JSON |
1248	| `copilot` / `cli:copilot` | `cli:copilot` descriptor `[ingest]`, including `COPILOT_DIR`, `session-state`, nested `events.jsonl`, and `data.context.cwd` | JSONL |
1249	| `pi` / `cli:pi` | `cli:pi` descriptor `[ingest]`, including `PI_CODING_AGENT_SESSION_DIR`, top-level `cwd`, and Pi session-header validation | JSONL |
1250	| `cursor` | `~/.cursor/chats/` (`DEADRECKON_IMPORT_CURSOR_ROOT`) | SQLite via `sqlite3 -json` |
1251	
1252	The command surface is `deadreckon import <source> [--preview|--list|--session <id-or-path>|--cwd <path>|--all|--since <duration>|--replace|--json]`. Default import filters candidates to the launch cwd or `--cwd` where the descriptor supports cwd matching. Empty, stale, and ambiguous candidate sets refuse without creating a run and print concrete `try:` lines. `--preview` and `--list` never create run directories. `--all` is the explicit whole-root mode.
1253	
1254	The handler creates an `imported-<hash>` run id from the concrete source-session identity, parses selected transcript files, appends normalized source-neutral entries to `traces.jsonl`, writes file provenance to `provenance.jsonl`, marks the run `Completed` (skipping the gate), and writes `import.json` under the run root. The manifest records `source`, `source_alias`, `schema`, `storage`, `cwd`, `mode`, `session_id`, `session_paths`, `content_hash`, source time bounds, row/event/provenance counts, `raw_rows_stored = false`, and the `deadreckon import ... --replace` command needed to reimport. If an existing imported run has a different content hash, import refuses unless `--replace` is explicit.
1255	
1256	Trace `detail` rows use a stable import schema: `import_version`, canonical `source`, `schema`, optional `session_id`, `source_path`, optional `source_line`, `source_event`, optional `role`, `summary`, optional tool fields, `files`, optional token `usage`, and `raw_hash`. Raw provider payloads are not copied into every trace row by default; source path/line plus hashes preserve auditability. Parser coverage includes Codex agent messages/function calls/token counts, Claude content/tool blocks, Gemini JSON/JSONL messages/tool calls, OpenCode file-mode sessions/messages/parts, Copilot assistant/reasoning/tool/usage rows, Pi session/message/tool/result rows, and Cursor SQLite rows.
1257	
1258	`deadreckon import` is the *user-driven* ingest. The *TUI-driven* ingest path that lets `attach` read live provider transcripts uses the same descriptor `[ingest]` roots, env overrides, storage kinds, file globs, freshness windows, cwd matching, and schema keys for CLI providers; see §18.3 and `docs/design/PROVIDER-CLI-INGEST.md`. OpenCode SQLite, provider transcript mutation/undo, full replay UI, and cross-run import analytics remain V1 candidates in `docs/V1-CANDIDATES.md`.
1259	
1260	---
1261	
1262	## 17. CLI Surface
1263	
1264	The `Commands` enum in `crates/deadreckon/src/cli.rs` defines the CLI surface; handlers live in `crates/deadreckon/src/main.rs`. Verbs and roles (line numbers are intentionally omitted — `cli.rs` is the source of truth and grows over time):
1265	
1266	Default top-level help presents the production model: `start`, `attach`,
1267	`status`, `list`, `finish`, `doctor`, `init`, `def-done`, `kill`, `resume`,
1268	`cleanup`, `help-all`, and `<command> --help`. Power-user launchers and
1269	building-block verbs remain callable, documented by `help-all`, exposed through
1270	their own `--help`, and available to completions, but they are no longer the
1271	first screen.
1272	
1273	| Verb | Role |
1274	|---|---|
1275	| `init` | Interactive setup of `~/.deadreckon/config.toml` |
1276	| `config get/set` | Non-interactive TOML edits |
1277	| `start` | Guided production front door for choosing and launching a run, follow-up, or orchestration path |
1278	| `run` | Advanced direct one-run launcher; create + enter turn loop |
1279	| `doctor` | Actionable preflight (OS, sandbox, providers, config, disk, runtime) |
1280	| `status` / `next` | Current project's latest run, locations, and next action |
1281	| `list` | Project-scoped run inventory by default; `--all` for global history, `--full` for exact values |
1282	| `apply` | Apply a completed worktree run (or merged plan result) to the user's current branch |
1283	| `finish` | Choose the right completion action (apply for git worktrees, export for non-git) for a run or merged plan |
1284	| `abandon` / `discard` | Remove a run's worktree branch/path or mark no-op modes abandoned |
1285	| `materialize` / `export` | Copy a completed fresh/copy artifact (or merged plan result) to a normal directory |
1286	| `cleanup` / `prune` | Clean abandoned, stale, or selected completed worktree runs |
1287	| `attach` | TUI on a live or completed run, chain, or plan |
1288	| `kill` | Lock release + child PID termination (run, chain, or plan) |
1289	| `resume` | Re-enter the loop on a non-Completed run |
1290	| `extend` | Re-open a completed run with a follow-up goal that inherits history |
1291	| `undo` | Restore snapshot to a target turn |
1292	| `rewind` | Preview or apply a provider flight checkpoint rewind (see §33) |
1293	| `show` | Pretty-print full state + provenance + traces; `--why-failed` for runs and plans; `--flight` / `--file` for the flight recorder |
1294	| `import` | Read-only descriptor-backed transcript import from CLI providers plus Cursor SQLite |
1295	| `chain` | Create, plan, run, attach, pause/resume/kill, undo, extend, and redo serial autonomous chains |
1296	| `orchestrate` | Advanced one-command wrappers for `review` and `full-plan` multi-agent runs |
1297	| `plan` | Advanced building block that writes an orchestration plan (worker specs + `plan.json`) without starting child runs |
1298	| `fork` | Advanced building block that spawns ready child runs for a plan and supervises them through completion |
1299	| `merge` | Advanced building block that composes completed child library artifacts into a new promoted run (with semantic merge repair) |
1300	| `def-done` | Write, add, show, or check the project's English done criteria |
1301	| `acceptance` | Hidden compatibility surface for creating, explaining, or checking done criteria |
1302	| `doc` | Print run narrative, as-built, implementation decision ledger, or delta; with optional polish pass |
1303	| `history` | Search durable run traces and provenance (regex/scope/plan filters) |
1304	| `library` | Query promoted run artifacts by goal/date/scope |
1305	| `detect` | Probe registered providers and return availability and credential status |
1306	| `providers` | List provider routes, models, kind tokens, and the active selection |
1307	| `update` | Check for or route self-updates via npm, Homebrew, shell, Cargo, or source channel |
1308	| `completion` / `completions` | Generate or install shell tab-completion scripts (bash, zsh, fish, elvish, powershell) |
1309	| `learn` | Index local run evidence and propose deadreckon improvements (see §34) |
1310	| `improve` | Run evidence-backed deadreckon self-improvement candidates (see §34) |
1311	| `help-all` / `commands` | Show every command, including advanced ones hidden from short help |
1312	
1313	### 17.1 Guided first use
1314	
1315	`deadreckon start "<goal>"` is the guided production command. It is intentionally a thin CLI-layer decision helper, not a new runtime state machine: each invocation builds an ephemeral launch decision, prints the selected path and reason, and either previews or dispatches to the existing `run`, `extend`, and `orchestrate` handlers. In an interactive TTY, `start` uses normal terminal selection prompts for launch mode, provider route, done criteria, source mode, and final confirmation when flags have not already made those choices explicit. No `PipelineState` schema changes were introduced for this path, and previews remain state-free.
1316	
1317	The launch decision resolves provider setup, done criteria, source mode, history, and run-vs-orchestrate mode before any provider work begins. Provider resolution uses configured defaults first and only probes installed subscription CLIs when no default route is configured; TTY users can select a detected route ephemerally for that launch without writing config, while non-TTY or scripted users still get concrete `try:` lines for `init`, `detect`, `config provider`, or `providers list --all`. Done-criteria resolution uses the same `def-done` and `.deadreckon/acceptance.yaml` contract as direct runs: existing project criteria trigger a TTY keep/view/check/update/cancel prompt so users can inspect or change the contract before launch, missing criteria can be generated or defaulted, and non-TTY callers get deterministic recovery lines. Source-mode resolution follows the existing run safety posture: git worktree by default in repositories, TTY selection for init-git/copy/fresh in non-git directories, and explicit stash or `--allow-dirty` choices for dirty worktrees.
1318	
1319	History-aware `start` scans the current project scope for the newest completed, promoted, non-in-place run. When one exists, the TTY launch picker adds a "Follow up" choice that dispatches through `extend`; preview and JSON output also include exact commands for `deadreckon extend <run-id> "<goal>"`, `deadreckon start "<goal>" --mode review --yes`, and `deadreckon start "<goal>" --mode full-plan --yes`. This keeps scripted `start` deterministic while making it obvious how to continue prior work or launch a new orchestration pass.
1320	
1321	Auto mode is deterministic in alpha. It chooses single-run, review orchestration, or full-plan orchestration from local goal text and explicit flags, then reports the override flag (`--mode run`, `--mode review`, or `--mode full-plan`) a user can pass if the heuristic guessed wrong. In a TTY, the recommendation appears first in the mode picker and the user can override it with a selection. The guided command does not ask a provider to classify the goal and does not persist personal preferences.
1322	
1323	`start --preview`, `run --preview`, and `orchestrate --preview` share launch-preview rows: path, provider, done criteria, workspace, watch, stop, and finish, with optional base/history rows when a follow-up is selected or available. Orchestrated `start` previews also show the alpha role reuse when one selected provider route is used for coder/reviewer or planner/child roles. Successful guided launches add a `start lifecycle` footer with exact `attach`, `status`, `kill`, and `finish` commands for the created run or plan. Existing `run`, `extend`, and `orchestrate` remain the canonical direct commands for users who already know the path they want.
1324	
1325	Prompt eligibility is deliberately narrow: `--json`, `--plain`, `--quiet`, `--yes`, and non-TTY execution never start the picker and never block on stdin. Those paths preserve deterministic JSON/recovery output and scriptable launch behavior. `--preview` may ask TTY users for selections, but it remains state-free; provider config is not written by a provider selection, and done-criteria files are only generated for an actual launch after final confirmation.
1326	
1327	The CLI defaults are honest: `--sandbox` defaults to `auto`, `--max-spend` defaults to `$10` (with a confirmation gate above `$50`), `--provider` defaults to the highest-credentialed entry per the fallback chain, `--skill` defaults to `default-coding`.
1328	
1329	`run` now starts codebase-aware by default. In a git repo it previews and then creates a `git worktree` on a `dr/...` branch; `--fresh` preserves the old empty-working-dir behavior, `--from <path>` uses copy mode, and `--in-place --i-know-its-a-lot` edits the source tree directly. Completed worktree runs hint `apply` / `discard`; copy and fresh runs hint `export` / `extend`. Run-id arguments accept unique prefixes and `latest` / `last` resolves to the latest run in the current project scope.
1330	
1331	`completion install` is driven from the real clap command tree, so subcommand aliases, flags, and value-hint completions stay in sync with `deadreckon --help`. The handler detects the active shell via `$SHELL`, writes the script to a per-shell default path (e.g. `~/.zsh/completions/_deadreckon`, `~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/deadreckon`), and for zsh adds a managed `# deadreckon completion` block to `~/.zshrc` unless `--no-rc` is passed. `init` invokes `try_install_completion_after_init` so first-time setup ships completions opt-out (`init --no-completion`). The per-shell stdout variants (`completion bash|zsh|fish|elvish|powershell`) print the script for users who manage their own shell config.
1332	
1333	`run` startup details (`print_run_started`) are now also emitted at the top of `extend` and `resume` so extended/resumed runs surface their selected provider route and doc-provider source the same way fresh runs do. Interactive terminals receive a `deadreckoning_course` ASCII progress strip and a polled `cli_wait_status` line while a long turn is in flight; the status is cleared as soon as the loop reports back. `kill` against a loaded run now also persists `RunStatus::Killed` + `killed_at` + `failure_reason = "killed by user"` before returning so downstream tooling sees a consistent terminal state.
1334	
1335	---
1336	
1337	## 18. TUI (`attach`)
1338	
1339	`attach_command` lives at `main.rs:18043`; `attach_tui` / `attach_tui_with_parent` at `main.rs:23560`/`23580`; the layout and collectors follow (`attach_panel_layout`, `collect_acceptance_live`, `collect_provider_activity`). `main.rs` is ~31k lines, so treat these line numbers as approximate locators.
1340	
1341	### 18.1 Behavior
1342	
1343	- On a TTY: `attach_tui()` enables raw mode, alternate screen, and renders a `ratatui` UI.
1344	- Off-TTY: prints a plain-text summary + locations.
1345	
1346	`attach` dispatches by id kind: a run id opens the run TUI documented below, a chain id opens the chain attach view (`Chains`, §28), and a plan id opens the plan attach TUI (`Plans`, §30.3 / §32.3). All three TUIs draw from the same palette (`ui::TUI_PALETTE`, §26.7) and the same key conventions (`q`/`Esc`/`Ctrl-D` detach; `d` toggles docs view in the run TUI; `Enter` drills into a child run from plan attach).
1347	
1348	`attach <id> --view narrative` adds a calmer operator projection for runs, plans, and plan child refs. The default remains `activity`, so raw tool/provider lines still open first unless the user requests the narrative view. In narrative mode, `n` toggles back to raw activity, `v` cycles `architecture -> agents -> files -> evidence -> none`, and `r` requests a provider-backed refresh when a configured route is available. While the TTY narrative view is open, meaningful run and plan events also request a provider refresh: errors, completions, tool milestones, docs checkpoints, acceptance running/pass/fail transitions, child-run discovery, task terminal states, and merge-repair milestones. Long-running quiet periods request a refresh after the narrative quiet window when the run or plan is still running. Provider refreshes are background jobs: manual/event/quiet refreshes coalesce while one is active, `q`/`Esc`/`Ctrl-D` detach remains immediate, and child drill-in from plan attach cancels or suspends the in-flight narrator before opening the child run. Provider refreshes are bounded: the prompt is built from redacted evidence windows, the provider must return strict cited JSON, graph labels may only target deterministic graph ids, and failures persist a stale deterministic projection instead of breaking attach.
1349	
1350	### 18.2 Layout
1351	
1352	`attach_panel_layout` (`main.rs:24166`):
1353	
1354	```rust
1355	let vertical = Layout::default()
1356	    .direction(Direction::Vertical)
1357	    .constraints([
1358	        Constraint::Length(5),    // top band: header + spend (if metered) + context + acceptance
1359	        Constraint::Min(10),      // tool calls + provider activity + live files
1360	        Constraint::Length(4),    // processes/status
1361	        Constraint::Length(2),    // keybindings footer (multi-line during long ops)
1362	    ])
1363	    .split(area);
1364	```
1365	
1366	The top band is split horizontally into three panels for subscription providers (header 66 / context 17 / acceptance 17) and four for metered API providers (header 55 / spend 15 / context 15 / acceptance 15):
1367	
1368	- **Header** (short run id, status, phase, provider, sandbox, turn timer, truncated goal, working/artifact path; degrades to an identity strip when live status is unavailable).
1369	- **Spend meter** only for metered API providers; CLI subscription providers omit cost and emphasize context/wall time.
1370	- **Context meter**: compact token/window summary with green/yellow/red thresholds.
1371	- **Acceptance meter**: derived from `AcceptanceLive` (`collect_acceptance_live` in `main.rs:24615`). When `proofs/acceptance-progress.jsonl` exists, the panel tails it and surfaces `running 2/5`, `passed`, or `failed` with the offending check; once `turn-acceptance.json` is signed, it pivots to a marker view (`acceptance_live_from_marker`). Color thresholds are owned by `acceptance_color`.
1372	- **Center, left**: wide streaming list of tool calls + provider activity + recent events. Acceptance lines from `acceptance_activity_lines` are interleaved so the operator sees the same progress in the activity stream and the meter.
1373	- **Narrative view**: `--view narrative` or `n` swaps the center-left activity pane for prose sections under the `Narrated` operator heading: freshness/coverage, headline, current work, architecture notes, risks, next likely action, and citations. Wide terminals split that pane with a right-side visual map; narrow terminals collapse to prose first. Run narratives cite `proofs/acceptance-progress.jsonl` or `proofs/turn-acceptance.json` when acceptance evidence exists, so failed done criteria point at the durable proof artifact. Plain/off-TTY narrative attach prints the same projection with citations and ASCII map lines when `--visual` is not `none`; `--json --view narrative` emits the structured state, snapshot, and graph objects. Non-TTY narrative attach stays deterministic and does not call a provider unless a future explicit refresh surface opts in. Chain narrative attach currently returns an unsupported response with `try:` lines for run and plan narrative attach.
1374	- **Completed docs view**: pressing `d` toggles the center-left panel from provider activity or narrative view to `RUN-NARRATIVE.md` rendered through `pulldown-cmark` into ratatui `Line`/`Span`s. Headings, bullets, inline code, fenced code blocks, links, task markers, math, and horizontal rules receive terminal styles and remain scrollable. The docs view remains a separate completed-run artifact rather than being merged into the live narrative projection.
1375	- **Center, right**: narrower live files list with count/bytes in the panel title.
1376	- **Bottom**: supervised PIDs + their `ps` lines (alive/dead annotation).
1377	- **Footer**: action-first completed footer (`[d] Docs` / `[d] Activity`, `[a] Apply`, `[b] Abandon`, `[s] Show`) or scroll/detach help while running. The footer's second line carries `deadreckoning_status_line` while long operations are in flight.
1378	
1379	### 18.3 Data source and responsiveness contract
1380	
1381	Each attach surface runs a budgeted tick loop. The render path is pure: it must not call providers, recurse through provider roots, append narrative snapshots, or reread unbounded JSONL files. Slow or potentially blocking work is either moved into an attach-owned cache/tailer or into a background refresh job whose completion is polled between frames.
1382	
1383	Run attach uses `TuiEventFeed` for run events and `AttachJsonlTail` for `spend.jsonl`, `traces.jsonl`, and `flight-events.jsonl`, so redraws parse only appended complete rows after the first load and ignore partial trailing JSONL until it is complete. Live-file collection uses an attach-specific inventory walker that prunes heavy cache/profile directories before descent and caps displayed rows without losing total counts. Provider activity prefers current flight rows; descriptor-backed provider-log fallback scans are throttled by freshness, matched path, root mtime, and file mtime so a live attach does not recursively scan provider homes every frame.
1384	
1385	`collect_provider_activity` resolves provider ingest through descriptor `[ingest]` metadata: candidate roots, env overrides, cwd matching, storage kind, file glob, freshness window, and schema key. `deadreckon import` reuses the same descriptor metadata for provider transcript discovery and adds import-only session selection, manifest writing, and normalized trace/provenance event creation. `cli:codex` reads `~/.codex/sessions/**.jsonl` and matches `session_meta.payload.cwd`; `cli:claude-code` reads `~/.claude/projects/<cwd-slug>/*.jsonl` using Claude Code's path-to-project mapping and matches top-level `cwd`; `cli:gemini` reads Gemini JSON/JSONL file logs; `cli:opencode` reads OpenCode file-mode `storage/session`, `storage/message`, and `storage/part` JSON; `cli:copilot` reads `~/.copilot/session-state/*.jsonl` plus nested `events.jsonl` and matches `data.context.cwd`; `cli:pi` reads `~/.pi/agent/sessions/<encoded-cwd>/*.jsonl`, validates the first nonblank row is a Pi `session`, and matches the header `cwd`. Schema-specific adapters only decode rows into common activity lines (`agent`, `thinking`, `tool`, `result`, `todo`, `tokens`) and normalize tool labels through `deadreckon_providers::taxonomy`.
1386	
1387	Production run attaches — same-process and cross-process alike — read run events by tailing `events.jsonl` via `TuiEventFeed::file_tail`; `TuiEventFeed::from_broadcast` is `#[cfg(test)]` only. (The loop's `emit_event` writes the file and sends on the `RunEventBus` channel together, so the file tail stays current; the broadcast path is reserved for a future same-process attach.) Plan attach consumes `PlanEventBus` / `PlanEventFeed`, which owns `plan-events.jsonl` replay/tailing, emits plan snapshots, tolerates malformed or partial plan-event rows, and multiplexes discovered child and repair run `events.jsonl` streams into the plan activity pane. Chain attach keeps its own `AttachJsonlTail<ChainEvent>` for `chain-events.jsonl`, preserves the existing drill/redo/extend/pause/kill controls, ignores partial last lines until complete, and shows an activity-read hint when chain event catch-up falls behind the tick budget. The production feeds remain durable-file backed for cross-process attach, with broadcast-capable APIs available for same-process streams.
1388	
1389	### 18.4 Narrative projection files
1390	
1391	Narrative attach writes projection files, not source-of-truth state. Run projections live under `<run-root>/narrative/`; plan projections live under `<plan-dir>/narrative/`.
1392	
1393	- `state.json` records the latest snapshot id/status, coverage, cadence, provider source, provider call count, cost/wall-clock accounting, and last refresh error.
1394	- `snapshots.jsonl` is append-only. Each row contains cited `current_work`, `architecture_notes`, `risks`, `next_likely`, citations, and plan-only agent/coordination sections. Malformed rows are skipped when reading the latest snapshot.
1395	- `architecture-graph.json` is a deterministic graph over run files, provider ids, checkpoints, plan tasks, dependencies, child runs, and citation ids. The TUI renders architecture, agent, file, and evidence views from this graph using ASCII-compatible labels and color-independent badges.
1396	
1397	Plan projections prefer each child run's latest narrative snapshot when one exists. The plan agent table cites that child snapshot and uses its headline as the child summary, then falls back to child run state when no child narrative exists. Plan graphs also roll up file nodes from child narrative graphs so the plan-level files visual can show cross-agent touched file evidence without copying child logs into `plan-events.jsonl`.
1398	
1399	Provider-backed narration is an overlay on these projections. Manual `r` refresh, TTY narrative-view event refreshes, and TTY narrative-view quiet-threshold refreshes start an asynchronous off-loop job (`tokio::spawn`); each attach tick only polls the job handle non-blockingly, so the render loop never stalls on a provider call. Provider refresh jobs build a redacted prompt from the deterministic projection, send only bounded evidence summaries to the selected provider route, validate all returned claims against known evidence ids, reject invented graph ids, and persist a new fresh snapshot only after validation. The default narrator route is `cli:claude-code` with model override `sonnet`, which the Claude Code adapter launches as `claude --model sonnet --dangerously-skip-permissions -p <prompt>`; `--narrative-provider` overrides the route and leaves model selection to that provider/config entry, while `--no-narrative-provider` keeps attach deterministic-only. Event refreshes can bypass the ordinary freshness interval for meaningful deltas, while quiet-threshold refreshes still obey the freshness interval; budget, provider availability, JSON validation, citation validation, graph validation, and redaction guards always apply. If the provider is missing, over budget, behind cadence, returns malformed JSON, cites unknown evidence, emits secret-like text, or fails, attach keeps running and persists a stale deterministic snapshot with the error in `state.json`.
1400	
1401	The run and plan narrative panes cache projection objects by coverage and feed signature. Redraws reuse the cached projection, stale provider snapshots survive ordinary frame churn, and render helpers fall back to deterministic projection builders instead of `ensure_*` persistence calls. This is the nonblocking attach contract: provider-backed narrative work may improve the next frame after it finishes, but it never owns the current frame.
1402

# Positioning Research: The Agent-Harness / Coding-Agent Landscape

## Part 1 — Competitor positioning audit (verbatim where available)

### Autonomous "AI software engineer" agents

**Devin (Cognition)** — the category-defining tagline.
- Headline: *"Introducing Devin, the first AI software engineer"*
- Verbatim: *"Devin is a tireless, skilled teammate, equally ready to build alongside you or independently complete tasks for you to review."* / *"Devin can plan and execute complex engineering tasks requiring thousands of decisions."* / equipped with *"the shell, code editor, and browser within a sandboxed compute environment."*
- Verbs/nouns: first, autonomous, plan, execute, end-to-end, sandboxed, teammate.
- Category: fully autonomous AI engineer (a "who," not a "what"). **Note: Devin already owns "sandboxed compute environment" + autonomy. deadreckon should not lead with sandbox alone.**

**Devika** — *"🚀 Devika - Agentic AI Software Engineer"* / *"the first open-source implementation of an Agentic Software Engineer."* Verbs: understand, break down, research, write. Explicit "open-source alternative to Devin."

**SWE-agent (Princeton/Stanford)** — *"SWE-agent takes a GitHub issue and tries to automatically fix it, using your LM of choice."* Positions on SWE-bench SOTA, "maximal agency to the LM," "simple & hackable." Research-grade autonomous fixer.

### Coding assistants / agents (terminal & IDE)

**Claude Code** — *"an agentic coding tool that lives in your terminal, understands your codebase, and helps you code faster by executing routine tasks, explaining complex code, and handling git workflows."* Verbs: lives, understands, helps, executes. Category: agentic coding tool (terminal-native).

**OpenAI Codex CLI** — *"Lightweight coding agent that runs in your terminal"* / *"a coding agent from OpenAI that runs locally on your computer."* Leans on: lightweight, local, runs in terminal.

**Cursor** — *"The best coding agent"* (formerly "The AI Code Editor"). Notable framing: the **"autonomy slider"** — *"you control how much independence to give the AI."* *"Agents use their own computers to build, test, and demo features end to end for you to review."*

**Aider** — *"AI Pair Programming in Your Terminal."* Verbs: pair program, build. Human-alongside framing, git-native.

**Cline** — *"The open source coding agent in your IDE and terminal."* / *"Autonomous coding agent as an SDK, IDE extension, or CLI assistant."* Emphasizes human-in-the-loop approval.

**Goose (Block)** — *"your native open source AI agent — desktop app, CLI, and API — for code, workflows, and everything in between"* / *"goes beyond code suggestions - install, execute, edit, and test with any LLM."* Leans on execute-not-suggest, extensible, MCP.

**Continue** — has pivoted to *"Source-controlled AI checks, enforceable in CI"* — runs review agents as GitHub status checks. (Interesting: moving toward the verification/enforcement space.)

**Tabby** — *"Self-hosted AI coding assistant"* — open-source/on-prem Copilot alternative. Differentiator is deployment, not autonomy.

**Sweep** — now *"AI coding assistant for JetBrains."* **Smol Developer** — *"the first library to let you embed a developer agent in your own app"* / "whole program synthesis." **gpt-engineer** — *"The OG code generation experimentation platform!"* — "specify software in natural language."

### Orchestration / multi-agent frameworks

**AutoGPT** — *"the vision of accessible AI for everyone"* / *"create, deploy, and manage continuous AI agents that automate complex workflows."* Build/Test/Delegate.

**AutoGen (Microsoft)** — *"A programming framework for agentic AI"* / "multi-agent AI applications that can act autonomously or work alongside humans." (Now in maintenance mode.)

**CrewAI** — *"Framework for orchestrating role-playing, autonomous AI agents… fostering collaborative intelligence."* / "Fast and Flexible Multi-Agent Automation Framework."

**MetaGPT** — *"The Multi-Agent Framework: First AI Software Company, Towards Natural Language Programming."* "Code = SOP(Team)."

### The directly competitive layer — harnesses / supervisors / parallel runners

This is where deadreckon actually lives, and it's the most important finding.

**ComposioHQ Agent Orchestrator** — *"The Orchestration Layer for Parallel AI Agents"* / *"Spawn parallel AI coding agents, each in its own git worktree. Agents autonomously fix CI failures, address review comments, and open PRs — you supervise from one dashboard."* Note: they use "you supervise," but the human supervises — there is no independent watchdog.

**Plandex** — *"An AI coding agent designed for large tasks and real world projects."* Has a *"cumulative diff review sandbox"* and claims *"full autonomy."* Closest on the "large/long" axis but the human is the reviewer.

**LangChain — "The Anatomy of an Agent Harness"** establishes the vocabulary that's now hardening: *"Agent = Model + Harness"*; the harness is *"every piece of code, configuration, and execution logic that isn't the model itself"*; provides *"state, tool execution, feedback loops, and enforceable constraints."* Key verbs: execute, **verify**, **persist**, orchestrate. **"Harness" as a category noun is becoming legible — deadreckon can credibly claim it.**

From the `awesome-cli-coding-agents` directory, the supervisor/verification framing is just beginning to surface in tiny projects:
- Aeon — *"runs unattended on GitHub Actions"*
- Galley — *"supervisor review against acceptance criteria"*
- Relay — *"supervised with live PR tracking + approval gates"*
- NemoClaw / Coasts / brood-box — sandbox/microVM isolation ("hardware-isolated microVM sandbox… egress control").

These confirm deadreckon's pillars exist as fragmented features in obscure tools, but **no prominent project bundles all four into a coherent value prop.**

---

## Part 2 — Synthesis

### The dominant positioning clichés (the overcrowded words)

1. **"AI software engineer" / "the first…"** — Devin, Devika, MetaGPT. Saturated and credibility-eroded.
2. **"agentic coding tool/agent"** — Claude Code, Codex, Cline, Cursor, Goose. The default noun phrase; now invisible.
3. **"in your terminal"** — Aider, Claude Code, Codex, Plandex. A location, not a value.
4. **"autonomous / full autonomy"** — everyone. The word has been so overused (by tools that still need babysitting) it now signals hype, not trust.
5. **"orchestrate / orchestration layer / multi-agent"** — AutoGen, CrewAI, MetaGPT, Composio. Framework-speak.
6. **"open source [alternative to X]"** — OpenHands, Devika, Tabby, Cline.
7. **"goes beyond suggestions / execute don't suggest"** — Goose, Devin, Cursor.
8. **"build, test, and ship/deploy end to end"** — Devin, Cursor, AutoGPT.
9. **"you supervise from one dashboard" / "human-in-the-loop approval"** — Composio, Cline, Relay. Note: supervision here always means *a human watching*, never *software that gates*.

Everyone leans on the same four words: **autonomous, agent, orchestrate, end-to-end.**

### The whitespace (where deadreckon's four pillars are uncontested)

| deadreckon pillar | Crowded? | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| **Unattended for long stretches** | Mostly empty | Devin/Composio imply it; nobody centers "unattended" as the promise. The honest "I ran it overnight / for 13 days" discourse is all in *blog posts*, not product positioning. |
| **Isolated sandboxes** | Owned by Devin (compute), worktree-tools | Don't lead here. Use as a supporting proof, not the headline. |
| **Un-foolable done-gate (agent can't mark its own work complete)** | **WIDE OPEN** | This is the strongest finding. Every competitor that "verifies" does so via the agent's *self-report* or a human reviewer. The exact failure mode deadreckon solves — *"hallucinated completion / hallucinated progress,"* agents writing "tests passing" while the suite has syntax errors — is named in technical blogs but **owned by no product as positioning.** The framing *"the agent can't mark its own work done"* is genuinely differentiated. |
| **Durable, auditable artifact (not a chat transcript)** | Emerging, uncontested | "Agentic artifacts," "evidence bundles," "provenance" exist in *academic papers* (MAIF) and one tiny tool (recursive-mode: *"durable artifacts… instead of losing everything in chat history"*). No prominent product owns *"auditable artifact, not a transcript."* |

**The unifying whitespace: trust through independence.** The entire field is built on the agent (or a human) judging the agent. deadreckon's thesis — *a separate process the agent can't fool decides when it's done, and proves it* — is a categorically different claim. That's the wedge.

### Headline patterns that work vs. generic ones

**Work (concrete capability + named pain):**
- SWE-agent: *"takes a GitHub issue and tries to automatically fix it"* — concrete input→output.
- Composio: *"Running one AI agent in a terminal is easy. Running 30… is a coordination problem."* — names the pain, then sells the fix.
- Cursor's *"autonomy slider"* — a memorable mental model.

**Generic (a category label, no claim):**
- *"agentic coding tool that lives in your terminal"* — describes location/mechanism, not outcome.
- *"A programming framework for agentic AI"* — pure category.
- *"AI-Driven Development"* — could be anything.

Pattern: lead with the **problem the buyer already feels** ("I can't trust it to run unattended / it lies about being done") and a **concrete mechanism** (a separate watchdog, an evidence bundle), not a category noun.

### Concrete language recommendations for deadreckon

**Words to own (low-competition, on-thesis):**
- **"supervision harness"** / **"watchdog"** — "harness" is becoming legible (LangChain) but no one owns "supervision harness." "Watchdog" is concrete and unclaimed in this space.
- **"done-gate" / "the agent can't mark its own work done"** — your sharpest line. Ties directly to the named industry pain ("hallucinated completion").
- **"unattended"** — own it as the promise, not a footnote.
- **"auditable artifact, not a chat transcript"** — crisp, contrastive, uncontested.
- **"evidence"** / **"proof"** — the field says "autonomous"; you say "proof."

**Words to avoid or use sparingly:** "autonomous" (devalued), "AI software engineer" (saturated/cringe), "orchestrate" (framework cliché), "in your terminal" (table stakes), "build/test/ship end to end" (everyone).

**Headline directions (problem-first, mechanism-led, trust-framed):**
- *"Agents lie about being done. deadreckon won't let them."*
- *"Run your coding agent unattended — a separate watchdog decides when it's actually done."*
- *"The supervision harness for agent CLIs: isolated, unattended, and un-foolable. It ships proof, not a transcript."*
- *"Your agent can't grade its own homework."* (folksy version of the done-gate)
- *"Let it run overnight. Wake up to an auditable artifact, not a chat log."*

**Positioning statement (one line):**
> deadreckon is a supervision harness that runs agent CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor CLI) unattended in isolated sandboxes — where a separate watchdog, not the agent, decides when the work is done, and the output is a durable, auditable artifact instead of a chat transcript.

**The category sentence to repeat:** Wrap the existing agents (don't compete with them) → *"Bring your own agent. deadreckon is the harness that makes it safe to walk away."* This sidesteps the entire crowded "best agent" fight and stakes out the supervision/trust layer above it.

---

### Key competitive watch-outs
- **Devin** already owns "sandboxed" + autonomy — frame sandbox as a supporting feature, not the lead.
- **Continue** is drifting toward enforceable CI checks; **Composio** toward "you supervise." Both are adjacent — the defensible gap is *who/what does the judging*: deadreckon's answer (an independent watchdog the agent cannot fool + an artifact as evidence) is the part neither claims.
- The honest "I ran an agent unattended for N days" narrative is currently living in **blog posts** (dev.to, Medium, SitePoint), which means the demand is real and the product positioning for it is empty. That's the gap to fill.

---

## DEADRECKON: GROUND TRUTH BRIEF FOR COPYWRITING

### 1. One-Sentence Accurate Description

**deadreckon is a Rust CLI harness that runs unattended long-running coding tasks in a platform-native sandbox, writes durable provenance records after every turn, and gates completion via an external binary the agent cannot read or forge.**

---

### 2. Core Architecture & Loop — The Actual Mechanism

**Two-Layer Split (AS-BUILT §3):**
- **Rust binary** (`crates/deadreckon*`): owns state machines, locks, sandboxes, provider routing, acceptance gates, atomic file operations, and crash recovery.
- **Markdown skill** (`skills/default-coding/SKILL.md`): the agent-facing judgment layer; loaded at runtime and included in the prompt frame. The binary never introspects the skill.

**Durable State (AS-BUILT §4-5):**
- `state.json` is the single source of truth, persisted atomically (temp + rename + fsync) after every phase transition, snapshot, and spend record.
- Seven gap-numbered phases (0: init, 10: plan, 20: provider, 30: sandbox, 40: execute, 50: verify, 60: complete) leave room for future insertions without schema rewrites.
- `RunStatus` enum (Pending, Planned, Executing, Completed, Failed, Killed) transitions are guarded: **only Phase(60) reaching Completed can set RunStatus::Completed**, and only if the acceptance gate passes (§13).

**Worktree Isolation (AS-BUILT §5):**
- In git repos, `deadreckon run` creates `~/.deadreckon/worktrees/<scope>-<run-id>/` on a `dr/...` branch.
- The user's checkout is untouched until `deadreckon apply <run-id>`.
- Scope is derived from the nearest `.git` root and is stable per worktree (prevents cross-repo collisions).

**The Turn Loop (AS-BUILT §9, in `crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs`):**

```
For turn in 1..max_turns (cap=12):
  1. Snapshot the pre-turn working directory to snapshots/turn-<N>/
  2. Build the prompt (reads skill + history)
  3. Call the provider (HTTP or CLI sub-agent)
  4. Parse one action (Bash, WriteFile, Done, or CLI sub-agent)
  5. Execute in sandbox (platform-native: Seatbelt on macOS, bwrap on Linux)
  6. Append spend/trace/provenance/events to durable JSONL files
  7. Save state and history
  8. If action == Done:
     a. Invoke dr-gate (external binary) — cannot be skipped
     b. Validate the signed marker (fails if agent forged it)
     c. If gate passes: promote working/ → library/<scope>/<run-id>/
     d. Set Phase(60)=Completed (only path to RunStatus::Completed)
     e. Return Done
  9. Otherwise continue (or fail if max_turns exhausted)
```

**dr-gate Watchdog (AS-BUILT §13):**
- Standalone binary (`crates/deadreckon/src/bin/dr-gate.rs`).
- Reads `gate/nonce` — a UUID written at run-init that the agent **never has access to**.
- Computes signature over nonce + check results.
- Agent cannot forge the marker because it cannot read the nonce.
- Acceptance failures are **non-terminal**: the loop logs the failure, appends a corrective hint to history, and lets the agent revise on the next turn. Only max-turn exhaustion terminates the run if gate keeps failing.

**Atomic Promotion (AS-BUILT §8):**
- When gate passes, `promote_if_ready` atomically renames `working/` → `library/<scope>/<run-id>/` on the same filesystem (or copies for cross-filesystem mode).
- If the rename fails mid-flight, `recover_promotion()` idempotently finishes the job on next run.
- The promotion is load-bearing: no run reaches `Completed` status without it.

**Crash Recovery (AS-BUILT §7):**
- Advisory OS-level file lock at `~/.deadreckon/locks/<scope>--<task_key>.lock`.
- Lock holds a `LockState` JSON with PID + timestamp.
- Stale detection: `pid_is_alive(pid)` (via `nix::kill` signal 0) + age > 30 min.
- Next run reclaims stale lock, overwrites PID, continues from `state.json` (which was synced before the crash).

---

### 3. Genuinely Differentiated Capabilities

**Anti-Self-Attestation Gate:**
The agent LLM cannot mark a run as done. The gate nonce is stored in plaintext on disk but **only the external dr-gate binary reads it**; the agent process never receives it. The binary refuses to write the acceptance marker if the signature doesn't validate. This is not a trust boundary you can re-architect (it's built into the file permissions and process isolation).

**Per-Turn Snapshots + Bounded Rollback:**
Every turn's working directory is captured to `snapshots/turn-<N>/` before executing that turn's tools. `deadreckon undo --run <id> --turn N` restores to any prior turn without replaying the full run. The snapshot is full-tree, not a diff — no merge logic needed, no lost context, but storage overhead is paid per turn.

**Provider Flight Recorder (AS-BUILT §33):**
For CLI sub-agents (e.g., `cli:codex`), a sidecar process polls the provider's live logs and the working tree, checkpoints deltas, and emits rewind events. This lets the operator rewind a Codex session mid-run from the TUI without re-running prior turns. HTTP providers do not have readable live logs, so the flight recorder is CLI-only.

**Durable Spend + Wall-Clock Metering:**
- HTTP providers: token counts + USD cost recorded per turn in `spend.jsonl`.
- CLI sub-agents: wall-clock seconds recorded (subscription, no token counts).
- Both cap types: `--max-spend <USD>` and `--max-wall-seconds <secs>` pause (not fail) a run.
- Spend is read from state after every turn; a cap exceeded pauses the run and leaves it resumable.

**Read-Only Cross-Tool Import:**
`deadreckon import codex|claude-code|cursor` reads transcripts from Codex sessions, Claude Code projects, and Cursor SQLite chats **without modifying the source**. Creates synthetic `imported-<hash>` runs with normalized provenance. This is purely ingest, not a migration tool — the original tool's session remains intact.

**Sandbox is Platform-Native, Not Daemon-Based:**
- macOS: `sandbox-exec` with generated Seatbelt profiles (SSH denied, network scoped, filesystem allowlists).
- Linux: `bwrap` with tmpfs `$HOME`, bind mounts, PID/network namespaces, no daemon.
- Docker: opt-in, no `bollard` (Docker CLI only).
- No Lima, no `docker-desktop-socket`, no background daemon.
- Each run gets its own profile/container, no state leakage between runs.

---

### 4. Unique Vocabulary & Concepts

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Dead reckoning** | Navigation by calculating position from known starting point and velocity, without external fixes. Applied here: the run continues from durable state on disk without replaying prior turns, using recorded history as the "known starting point." |
| **def-done** | Plain-English project-scoped done criteria. User writes `deadreckon def-done "build, test, and deploy"` → provider converts to `acceptance.yaml` (file checks, build checks, shell checks, etc.). Same contract applies to every run in the project. |
| **dr-gate** | External binary that validates done criteria and signs the acceptance marker. The name echoes the "gate" concept: a pass/fail checkpoint the agent cannot bypass. |
| **Chain** | Serial autonomous goal-chaining: user sets one goal, agent completes it, autonomously proposes the next refinement/feature/fix, and repeats until the chain is abandoned or a max-chain-length cap is hit. The chain stores conductor state and decision points. |
| **Provenance** | File-level origin tracking: which prompt/turn/model produced this file? Answered by `provenance.jsonl` — one line per file-change with turn ID, tool call ID, and model name. |
| **Flight recorder** | Sidecar process that polls CLI sub-agent logs + working tree deltas and emits checkpoint events. Used by `rewind` to preview/apply mid-run rollback of a Codex session. |
| **Rewind** | Preview or apply a provider flight checkpoint to restore the working tree to an earlier turn without re-running. CLI-only (Codex/Claude Code logs are readable; HTTP API responses are not). |
| **Learn / improve** | Local self-improvement loop (alpha): evidence-based indexing of prior runs, signal generation, proposal generation, candidate evaluation, and feedback. Proposals live under `~/.deadreckon/learning/`. |
| **Acceptance marker** | Signed JSON proof that done criteria passed. Location: `<run_root>/proofs/turn-acceptance.json`. Signature covers the nonce (only dr-gate can read it) + check results. |
| **Worktree mode** | (vs. copy/fresh/in-place) Default in git repos: `deadreckon` creates a separate `git worktree` on a `dr/...` branch so the agent's edits don't touch your checkout. |
| **Scope** | Stable identifier for a project/directory. Derived from nearest `.git` root + fnv1a32 hash. Used to group runs, locks, and chains per project. |
| **Promotion** | Atomic rename/copy of the completed run from `runstate/<scope>/runs/<run-id>/working/` → `library/<scope>/<run-id>/`. Only happens after the gate passes and before the run is marked `Completed`. |

---

### 5. What the Target User Actually Gets

**Artifacts (in `~/.deadreckon/`):**
- **Completed run library** (`library/<scope>/<run-id>/`): the working tree after the agent finished, plus a `manifest.json` recording provenance hash and promotion timestamp.
- **Durable audit trail** (`spend.jsonl`, `traces.jsonl`, `provenance.jsonl`, `events.jsonl`): every LLM call, tool invocation, file change, and spend delta, with latencies and error details.
- **Run narrative docs** (`RUN-NARRATIVE.md`, `RUN-AS-BUILT.md`, `IMPLEMENTATION-DECISIONS.md`): automatically generated by `default-coding` skill + optional polish pass. Readable in the TUI (`d` key).
- **Acceptance evidence** (`proofs/turn-acceptance.json`, `acceptance-progress.jsonl`): the signed marker proving done criteria passed, plus streaming progress while the gate runs.
- **Snapshots** (`snapshots/turn-<N>/`): full working-tree copies at each turn boundary, enabling undo without replay.

**CLI Control & Visibility:**
- `deadreckon run "goal"` — create, enter loop, attach TUI when done.
- `deadreckon attach <id>` — live TUI dashboard with spend meter, context, acceptance meter, provider activity, files, processes.
- `deadreckon show <id>` — full state + provenance + traces in pretty-printed JSON.
- `deadreckon status` / `deadreckon list` — project scope inventory.
- `deadreckon apply <id>` (worktree) / `deadreckon export <id> --dest ./dir` (copy/fresh) — graduate the artifact.
- `deadreckon kill <id>` / `deadreckon resume <id>` — supervise in-flight runs.
- `deadreckon undo <id> --turn N` — restore a prior snapshot.
- `deadreckon extend <id> "follow-up goal"` — continue from a completed run (preserves lineage and history).
- `deadreckon def-done` — view/edit project done criteria.

**Sandbox & Provider Routing:**
- Platform-native sandboxes (Seatbelt / bwrap) with per-run profiles.
- BYOK provider routing: fallback chain from local CLI (Claude Code, Codex) to HTTP API (Anthropic, OpenAI) to compatible endpoints.
- Subscription billing: CLI sub-agents only meter wall-clock; no token counts, no costs.
- `--max-spend $X --max-wall-seconds Y` pause runs at budget, not fail.

---

### 6. Honest Limitations & Scope

**Alpha Stage:**
- Feature completeness is explicit. `docs/V1-CANDIDATES.md` lists deferred work: provider transcript mutation, full replay UI, cross-run analytics, explicit multi-agent forks, V2+ features.
- Build/test coverage is green for the current slice; broad release stress verification remains an explicit operator choice.
- TUI narrative view requires `--narrative-provider` flag; deterministic narrative (no provider call) is the default for stability.

**What's Not Built:**
- **Automatic provider detection and setup.** `deadreckon init` is interactive; non-TTY users must pass explicit flags.
- **Multi-agent forking from one goal.** Alpha records scope/session lineage and keeps the subprocess skill boundary. Explicit `deadreckon fork` or `deadreckon orchestrate` workflows are documented but feature-light.
- **Undo for provider actions.** Snapshots let you restore the working tree, but the provider's internal session state (if it's a CLI sub-agent) is not rewound unless you explicitly use `deadreckon rewind`.
- **Live provider log mutation.** Codex logs are read-only; the flight recorder observes but does not edit them.
- **Cross-provider fallback attestation.** If HTTP provider A fails and falls back to provider B, the accepted run records provider B's ID, not both. No runtime fallback cost accounting.

**Sandbox Limitations:**
- **`None` backend is unsafe.** The CLI accepts `--sandbox none` but warns and requires explicit understanding. No automatic fallback to safer sandboxes.
- **Docker is opt-in.** The harness prefers `sandbox-exec` / `bwrap` and only shells to `docker` if explicitly selected or auto-selected on an unsupported platform with no alternatives.
- **Read-allowlists are conservative.** The working directory and a fixed list of system paths (e.g., `/usr/lib`, `/opt`) are readable. Broader read access requires explicit `--sandbox none`.

**Gate Limitations:**
- **Acceptance checks are simple.** Supported kinds: `file_exists`, `content_match` (regex or substring), `cargo_test`, `build_success` (generic shell build), `shell` (user script). No semantic code analysis, no syntax validation, no AI-driven outcome prediction.
- **Acceptance is non-terminal only during the run.** Once the turn budget is exhausted, the run fails; the agent cannot make a new attempt from the CLI — a new run is required.

**Import Limitations:**
- **Read-only, not migratory.** Cross-tool imports create synthetic completed runs; they do not move or transform the source tool's session.
- **Partial schema coverage.** Some CLI tools (e.g., Cursor) are ingested via SQLite; others (Codex, Claude Code) via JSONL. Not all fields are captured; raw payloads are hashed, not stored.

---

### 7. Strongest 3-5 Proof Points

1. **Nonce-Guarded Acceptance Signature (§13).**  
   The gate nonce is written at run-init in plaintext but stored in a file the agent never receives. Only `dr-gate` reads it; the binary refuses to write a marker without the correct signature. An LLM cannot forge a marker because it cannot read `gate/nonce`. This is not a suggestion or a promise—it's an explicit file-I/O boundary enforced at the OS level. Copywriting should emphasize: "The acceptance marker is signed by a separate binary the agent cannot read, making self-attestation impossible."

2. **Atomic Promotion + Crash Recovery (§8, §7).**  
   Promotion is a single `rename()` call on the same filesystem (or copy for cross-filesystem). If the process dies mid-promotion, the next run's `recover_promotion()` idempotently finishes the job. The run state is synced to disk before every phase transition, so a crash never leaves `state.json` in a half-written state. Copywriting: "If the agent crashes or you kill the run, the next resume picks up from the exact point in state.json where it stopped. No re-running, no replay, no lost context."

3. **Per-Turn Snapshots Without Replay (§9, §5).**  
   Every turn, the entire working directory is snapshotted to disk. `deadreckon undo --turn N` restores that snapshot instantly, with no re-execution. This is different from "undo the LLM prompt" (which is common in other tools) — you can rollback the **actual code changes**, not just the prompt. Copywriting: "Roll back code changes to any prior turn in seconds, without re-running earlier turns."

4. **Platform-Native Sandboxes, Not Docker-Daemon-Dependent (§11).**  
   Each run gets its own Seatbelt profile (macOS) or bwrap container (Linux). No shared daemon, no `bollard` SDK, no Lima VMs. Per-run isolation is enforced by the OS kernel, not a daemon. Copywriting: "Each run executes in a fresh, isolated sandbox generated just for that run. macOS uses Seatbelt profiles, Linux uses Bubblewrap—both kernel-level, not containerization."

5. **Durable Provenance: File → Prompt (§14.3).**  
   `provenance.jsonl` records which turn, tool call, model, and prompt produced each changed file. Running `deadreckon show <id> | grep src/main.rs` answers "which LLM call wrote this file?" This is load-bearing for audit trails and understanding agent reasoning. Copywriting: "Every changed file is linked to the exact turn, tool, and model that created it—full traceability from code back to prompt."

---

**Overall Frame for Copywriting:**

deadreckon is **the harness around your agent CLI, not a replacement for it**. It adds:
- **Durability**: every state transition, spend, and tool call is persisted to durable JSONL before the next step.
- **Verification**: done criteria are checked by an external binary the agent cannot trick.
- **Isolation**: platform-native sandboxes keep each run separate.
- **Rollback**: per-turn snapshots let you undo code changes without replaying earlier work.
- **Audit**: file-level provenance answers which prompt created which code.

For teams already using Codex, Claude Code, or API CLIs, deadreckon provides the **supervision, observability, and recovery guarantees** those tools don't ship with. It's alpha, intentionally local-first, and built to outlast its providers.

**AI Agent Harness Concepts:**

bux is a 24/7 Claude Code agent with Browser Harness that demonstrates how to combine a terminal-native coding agent with live browser automation for unattended agents that need both shell and browser surfaces.

**Unattended Execution at Scale:**

Unattended AI work can operate at a meaningful production scale when placed inside a carefully managed environment. Systems oriented around unattended execution operate in a constrained engineering environment with human review retained as a control boundary.

**Supervisor and Verification:**

To prevent "hallucinated completion" where an agent falsely claims a task is done, harnesses use automated testing gates that physically block the agent from marking a task as complete until it passes tests. If a test fails, the harness automatically feeds the error back to the agent, forcing it to iterate and self-correct until the logic is verified.

The Verification Loop is the practice of having an agent run the team's own test suite, CI pipeline, and monitoring checks before submitting a PR.

**Real-World Implementation:**

258 self-healing actions is what unattended actually means in practice - the daemon caught and fixed its own stalls 258 times across 19 days without paging. 1,304 verification evidence bundles were collected before tasks were allowed near a merge, representing moments where the supervisor either kept itself alive or refused to ship something it couldn't justify.

# Agent Harness Definition and Key Vocabulary

## Core Definition

The article defines an agent harness as: **"Every piece of code, configuration, and execution logic that isn't the model itself."** The foundational equation is simple: **"Agent = Model + Harness."**

More specifically, the harness transforms a raw model into a functional agent by providing: **"state, tool execution, feedback loops, and enforceable constraints."**

## Concrete Harness Components

The article lists these specific elements:
- System prompts
- Tools, skills, and MCPs with descriptions
- Bundled infrastructure (filesystem, sandbox, browser)
- Orchestration logic (subagent spawning, handoffs, model routing)
- Hooks/middleware for deterministic execution

## Recurring Key Terms & Actions

**Primary nouns:** harness, model, filesystem, sandbox, tools, context, verification, planning

**Central verbs/actions:**
- **Execute** (code, tools, work)
- **Verify** (self-verification loops, test running)
- **Persist** (durable state across sessions)
- **Orchestrate** (subagent spawning, parallel delegation)
- **Inject** (context, memory, knowledge)
- **Compact** (manage context window overflow)
- **Observe** (results, logs, screenshots)

The article emphasizes that **"the model contains the intelligence and the harness is the system that makes that intelligence useful."**

Based on the search results, here are the key findings related to your query about agents marking their own work, hallucinated completions, and verification gates:

## The Core Problem: Self-Reporting Agents

Most orchestration tools that coordinate AI agents verify work by reading transcripts. The agent says "committed 3 files" or "all tests passing" and the verifier pattern-matches those strings as evidence of completion. That's trusting the agent's self-report.

Agents generate completion language as part of their output pattern regardless of the actual state of the codebase. An agent will write "tests passing" into its response while the test suite has syntax errors. It'll claim files were created that only exist in the prompt's hypothetical, not on disk.

## "Hallucinated Work" vs. Hallucinated Content

Hallucinated work is the failure mode that matters most. The more dangerous version is hallucinated progress — an agent that confidently reports what it did when it didn't do it. In a system where agent output is verified by the agent itself, this is undetectable.

## Verification Gate Solutions

The search results identify several approaches to prevent agents from self-verifying:

1. **Outcome-Based Verification**: The core move is shifting trust from transcript to artifact. An agent saying it changed files, passed tests, or completed the task is not evidence.

2. **Pre-Execution Review**: Pre-execution review (automated analysis of agent actions before they execute) fills the gap. Instead of asking a human to detect issues in real time, it runs structured checks or a reviewer agent that evaluates context, compares against known bad patterns, and surfaces specific findings — before the action runs.

3. **Acceptance Criteria Gates**: Gate every task completion with automated tests, linting, and type checks before allowing a commit. Commit after every completed task so rollback is always a single git revert.

4. **Separate Verification Agents**: If your agent system uses the same agent session to build and validate, you're asking the least reliable capability (self-assessment) to gate the output of a more reliable one (implementation). The architecture should have the build agent and the drift-check agent as separate invocations with separate contexts, and the compiler and test suite as the actual gates.

## Key Findings

**Agentic Artifacts & Auditability**

Agentic artifacts are persistent, structured outputs created by autonomous agents, ranging from code, documents, presentations, configuration files, analytical reports, and data bundles to executable proofs and workflow scripts. These artifacts are stored in machine-readable, versioned formats, explicitly linking to decision rationale, provenance, and supporting evidence.

**Beyond Chat Transcripts**

Recursive-mode provides audited phases, durable artifacts, and persistent memory instead of losing everything in chat history, keeping requirements, plans, implementation evidence, and decisions in repository files—making agent work auditable, resumable, and consistent across contributors.

**Provenance & Trust Framework**

An artifact-centric AI agent paradigm grounds behavior in persistent, verifiable data artifacts rather than ephemeral tasks. The Multimodal Artifact File Format (MAIF) is an AI-native container embedding semantic representations, cryptographic provenance, and granular access controls.

**Evidence Bundles for Audit**

Auditors and regulators demand an immutable, reproducible trail of data provenance, model lineage, and control evidence; automating the assembly of audit-ready folders reduces manual toil and strengthens governance. Each artifact policy event records the requested selector, resolved immutable identity, provenance result, verdict, evidence pointer, context, and expiry or revocation state—these durable events are the missing join key for recall, audit, and incident reconstruction.

**Research on Claim-Level Auditability**

The Auditable Autonomous Research (AAR) standard proposes semantic provenance with protocolized validation: persistent, queryable provenance graphs that encode claim-evidence relations and integrate continuous validation during synthesis.

# Positioning Research: The Agent-Harness / Coding-Agent Landscape

## Part 1 — Competitor positioning audit (verbatim where available)

### Autonomous "AI software engineer" agents

**Devin (Cognition)** — the category-defining tagline.
- Headline: *"Introducing Devin, the first AI software engineer"*
- Verbatim: *"Devin is a tireless, skilled teammate, equally ready to build alongside you or independently complete tasks for you to review."* / *"Devin can plan and execute complex engineering tasks requiring thousands of decisions."* / equipped with *"the shell, code editor, and browser within a sandboxed compute environment."*
- Verbs/nouns: first, autonomous, plan, execute, end-to-end, sandboxed, teammate.
- Category: fully autonomous AI engineer (a "who," not a "what"). **Note: Devin already owns "sandboxed compute environment" + autonomy. deadreckon should not lead with sandbox alone.**

**Devika** — *"🚀 Devika - Agentic AI Software Engineer"* / *"the first open-source implementation of an Agentic Software Engineer."* Verbs: understand, break down, research, write. Explicit "open-source alternative to Devin."

**SWE-agent (Princeton/Stanford)** — *"SWE-agent takes a GitHub issue and tries to automatically fix it, using your LM of choice."* Positions on SWE-bench SOTA, "maximal agency to the LM," "simple & hackable." Research-grade autonomous fixer.

### Coding assistants / agents (terminal & IDE)

**Claude Code** — *"an agentic coding tool that lives in your terminal, understands your codebase, and helps you code faster by executing routine tasks, explaining complex code, and handling git workflows."* Verbs: lives, understands, helps, executes. Category: agentic coding tool (terminal-native).

**OpenAI Codex CLI** — *"Lightweight coding agent that runs in your terminal"* / *"a coding agent from OpenAI that runs locally on your computer."* Leans on: lightweight, local, runs in terminal.

**Cursor** — *"The best coding agent"* (formerly "The AI Code Editor"). Notable framing: the **"autonomy slider"** — *"you control how much independence to give the AI."* *"Agents use their own computers to build, test, and demo features end to end for you to review."*

**Aider** — *"AI Pair Programming in Your Terminal."* Verbs: pair program, build. Human-alongside framing, git-native.

**Cline** — *"The open source coding agent in your IDE and terminal."* / *"Autonomous coding agent as an SDK, IDE extension, or CLI assistant."* Emphasizes human-in-the-loop approval.

**Goose (Block)** — *"your native open source AI agent — desktop app, CLI, and API — for code, workflows, and everything in between"* / *"goes beyond code suggestions - install, execute, edit, and test with any LLM."* Leans on execute-not-suggest, extensible, MCP.

**Continue** — has pivoted to *"Source-controlled AI checks, enforceable in CI"* — runs review agents as GitHub status checks. (Interesting: moving toward the verification/enforcement space.)

**Tabby** — *"Self-hosted AI coding assistant"* — open-source/on-prem Copilot alternative. Differentiator is deployment, not autonomy.

**Sweep** — now *"AI coding assistant for JetBrains."* **Smol Developer** — *"the first library to let you embed a developer agent in your own app"* / "whole program synthesis." **gpt-engineer** — *"The OG code generation experimentation platform!"* — "specify software in natural language."

### Orchestration / multi-agent frameworks

**AutoGPT** — *"the vision of accessible AI for everyone"* / *"create, deploy, and manage continuous AI agents that automate complex workflows."* Build/Test/Delegate.

**AutoGen (Microsoft)** — *"A programming framework for agentic AI"* / "multi-agent AI applications that can act autonomously or work alongside humans." (Now in maintenance mode.)

**CrewAI** — *"Framework for orchestrating role-playing, autonomous AI agents… fostering collaborative intelligence."* / "Fast and Flexible Multi-Agent Automation Framework."

**MetaGPT** — *"The Multi-Agent Framework: First AI Software Company, Towards Natural Language Programming."* "Code = SOP(Team)."

### The directly competitive layer — harnesses / supervisors / parallel runners

This is where deadreckon actually lives, and it's the most important finding.

**ComposioHQ Agent Orchestrator** — *"The Orchestration Layer for Parallel AI Agents"* / *"Spawn parallel AI coding agents, each in its own git worktree. Agents autonomously fix CI failures, address review comments, and open PRs — you supervise from one dashboard."* Note: they use "you supervise," but the human supervises — there is no independent watchdog.

**Plandex** — *"An AI coding agent designed for large tasks and real world projects."* Has a *"cumulative diff review sandbox"* and claims *"full autonomy."* Closest on the "large/long" axis but the human is the reviewer.

**LangChain — "The Anatomy of an Agent Harness"** establishes the vocabulary that's now hardening: *"Agent = Model + Harness"*; the harness is *"every piece of code, configuration, and execution logic that isn't the model itself"*; provides *"state, tool execution, feedback loops, and enforceable constraints."* Key verbs: execute, **verify**, **persist**, orchestrate. **"Harness" as a category noun is becoming legible — deadreckon can credibly claim it.**

From the `awesome-cli-coding-agents` directory, the supervisor/verification framing is just beginning to surface in tiny projects:
- Aeon — *"runs unattended on GitHub Actions"*
- Galley — *"supervisor review against acceptance criteria"*
- Relay — *"supervised with live PR tracking + approval gates"*
- NemoClaw / Coasts / brood-box — sandbox/microVM isolation ("hardware-isolated microVM sandbox… egress control").

These confirm deadreckon's pillars exist as fragmented features in obscure tools, but **no prominent project bundles all four into a coherent value prop.**

---

## Part 2 — Synthesis

### The dominant positioning clichés (the overcrowded words)

1. **"AI software engineer" / "the first…"** — Devin, Devika, MetaGPT. Saturated and credibility-eroded.
2. **"agentic coding tool/agent"** — Claude Code, Codex, Cline, Cursor, Goose. The default noun phrase; now invisible.
3. **"in your terminal"** — Aider, Claude Code, Codex, Plandex. A location, not a value.
4. **"autonomous / full autonomy"** — everyone. The word has been so overused (by tools that still need babysitting) it now signals hype, not trust.
5. **"orchestrate / orchestration layer / multi-agent"** — AutoGen, CrewAI, MetaGPT, Composio. Framework-speak.
6. **"open source [alternative to X]"** — OpenHands, Devika, Tabby, Cline.
7. **"goes beyond suggestions / execute don't suggest"** — Goose, Devin, Cursor.
8. **"build, test, and ship/deploy end to end"** — Devin, Cursor, AutoGPT.
9. **"you supervise from one dashboard" / "human-in-the-loop approval"** — Composio, Cline, Relay. Note: supervision here always means *a human watching*, never *software that gates*.

Everyone leans on the same four words: **autonomous, agent, orchestrate, end-to-end.**

### The whitespace (where deadreckon's four pillars are uncontested)

| deadreckon pillar | Crowded? | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| **Unattended for long stretches** | Mostly empty | Devin/Composio imply it; nobody centers "unattended" as the promise. The honest "I ran it overnight / for 13 days" discourse is all in *blog posts*, not product positioning. |
| **Isolated sandboxes** | Owned by Devin (compute), worktree-tools | Don't lead here. Use as a supporting proof, not the headline. |
| **Un-foolable done-gate (agent can't mark its own work complete)** | **WIDE OPEN** | This is the strongest finding. Every competitor that "verifies" does so via the agent's *self-report* or a human reviewer. The exact failure mode deadreckon solves — *"hallucinated completion / hallucinated progress,"* agents writing "tests passing" while the suite has syntax errors — is named in technical blogs but **owned by no product as positioning.** The framing *"the agent can't mark its own work done"* is genuinely differentiated. |
| **Durable, auditable artifact (not a chat transcript)** | Emerging, uncontested | "Agentic artifacts," "evidence bundles," "provenance" exist in *academic papers* (MAIF) and one tiny tool (recursive-mode: *"durable artifacts… instead of losing everything in chat history"*). No prominent product owns *"auditable artifact, not a transcript."* |

**The unifying whitespace: trust through independence.** The entire field is built on the agent (or a human) judging the agent. deadreckon's thesis — *a separate process the agent can't fool decides when it's done, and proves it* — is a categorically different claim. That's the wedge.

### Headline patterns that work vs. generic ones

**Work (concrete capability + named pain):**
- SWE-agent: *"takes a GitHub issue and tries to automatically fix it"* — concrete input→output.
- Composio: *"Running one AI agent in a terminal is easy. Running 30… is a coordination problem."* — names the pain, then sells the fix.
- Cursor's *"autonomy slider"* — a memorable mental model.

**Generic (a category label, no claim):**
- *"agentic coding tool that lives in your terminal"* — describes location/mechanism, not outcome.
- *"A programming framework for agentic AI"* — pure category.
- *"AI-Driven Development"* — could be anything.

Pattern: lead with the **problem the buyer already feels** ("I can't trust it to run unattended / it lies about being done") and a **concrete mechanism** (a separate watchdog, an evidence bundle), not a category noun.

### Concrete language recommendations for deadreckon

**Words to own (low-competition, on-thesis):**
- **"supervision harness"** / **"watchdog"** — "harness" is becoming legible (LangChain) but no one owns "supervision harness." "Watchdog" is concrete and unclaimed in this space.
- **"done-gate" / "the agent can't mark its own work done"** — your sharpest line. Ties directly to the named industry pain ("hallucinated completion").
- **"unattended"** — own it as the promise, not a footnote.
- **"auditable artifact, not a chat transcript"** — crisp, contrastive, uncontested.
- **"evidence"** / **"proof"** — the field says "autonomous"; you say "proof."

**Words to avoid or use sparingly:** "autonomous" (devalued), "AI software engineer" (saturated/cringe), "orchestrate" (framework cliché), "in your terminal" (table stakes), "build/test/ship end to end" (everyone).

**Headline directions (problem-first, mechanism-led, trust-framed):**
- *"Agents lie about being done. deadreckon won't let them."*
- *"Run your coding agent unattended — a separate watchdog decides when it's actually done."*
- *"The supervision harness for agent CLIs: isolated, unattended, and un-foolable. It ships proof, not a transcript."*
- *"Your agent can't grade its own homework."* (folksy version of the done-gate)
- *"Let it run overnight. Wake up to an auditable artifact, not a chat log."*

**Positioning statement (one line):**
> deadreckon is a supervision harness that runs agent CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor CLI) unattended in isolated sandboxes — where a separate watchdog, not the agent, decides when the work is done, and the output is a durable, auditable artifact instead of a chat transcript.

**The category sentence to repeat:** Wrap the existing agents (don't compete with them) → *"Bring your own agent. deadreckon is the harness that makes it safe to walk away."* This sidesteps the entire crowded "best agent" fight and stakes out the supervision/trust layer above it.

---

### Key competitive watch-outs
- **Devin** already owns "sandboxed" + autonomy — frame sandbox as a supporting feature, not the lead.
- **Continue** is drifting toward enforceable CI checks; **Composio** toward "you supervise." Both are adjacent — the defensible gap is *who/what does the judging*: deadreckon's answer (an independent watchdog the agent cannot fool + an artifact as evidence) is the part neither claims.
- The honest "I ran an agent unattended for N days" narrative is currently living in **blog posts** (dev.to, Medium, SitePoint), which means the demand is real and the product positioning for it is empty. That's the gap to fill.

Sources: GitHub READMEs for AutoGPT, Aider, OpenHands, SWE-agent, gpt-engineer, MetaGPT, AutoGen, CrewAI, Cline, Continue, Goose, Plandex, Codex, Sweep, smol-ai/developer, Tabby, Devika, claude-code, ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator, bradAGI/awesome-cli-coding-agents; cognition.ai/blog/introducing-devin; cursor.com; langchain.com "The Anatomy of an Agent Harness"; dev.to "AI coding agents lie about their work"; recursive-mode.dev; arxiv MAIF.
